stem: A parent of a 7-year-old asks whether it matters that a new tooth has erupted on one side only, with no matching tooth on the other side yet; what is the most accurate response?

options.text: Unilateral eruption of teeth should be questioned, because it may reflect pathology in the maxilla or mandible
This is the expected pattern for permanent tooth eruption and does not need to be questioned
It is only concerning if it happens before 6 months of age
It means the child should have more than 20 primary teeth
It confirms an odontogenic infection as the cause

explanation: Unilateral eruption of teeth should be questioned because asymmetry may indicate pathology in the maxilla or mandible.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes

rationale: The key teaching point is that tooth eruption should be bilateral and symmetric. A unilateral pattern warrants consideration of local pathology rather than being dismissed as normal variation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because unilateral eruption should prompt questioning for possible pathology in the maxilla or mandible.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because a unilateral pattern is not automatically expected and should not be ignored.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the concern is asymmetry of eruption, not an age threshold of 6 months.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because unilateral eruption does not imply an increased number of primary teeth.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because unilateral eruption alone does not confirm an odontogenic infection.
